newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Meyer set to abandon white opposition.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Meyer set to abandon white opposition.

text.p: A co-architect of South Africa's new order, Roelf Meyer, is expected to announce on Saturday that he will leave the former ruling National Party to work for a realignment of politics across the racial divide, analysts said.

Meyer, who played a crucial role in negotiating the peaceful handover of power from white rule this decade, attends a decisive meeting of the party on Saturday morning and called a press conference for 11 a.m. (0900 GMT). He said he would spell out his future plans.
At a Foreign Correspondents' Association luncheon on Friday, Meyer declined to comment directly on speculation of his resignation but said he had been pushed into rethinking his political fate.
"It was forced on me," he said. While he did not elaborate, Meyer -- once the golden boy of the "Nats" -- has effectively been sidelined by party hardliners who see him as too liberal.

His status was reduced to that of an ordinary MP this month after NP leader F.W. de Klerk took over a team that Meyer had led in search of a broad, moderate alliance to challenge the ruling African National Congress.

Mapping out his vision of a new political movement in South Africa, Meyer told foreign journalists the multi-racial democracy propounded in the post-apartheid constitution demanded a breakup of the old order.
"I would hate to see this country of ours not being able to really take through what is envisaged in our constitution. There is a huge opportunity if one has the right players," he added.

Meyer said a new political movement would not necessarily be viable by the general elections scheduled for 1999, but it would be feasible to set the foundations on which the political party scene could be restructured.
"South Africa is politically speaking still very much a racially divided country, unfortunately. There is baggage which, to my mind, calls for something new.
"This fluidity might just jell in something new and solid if there is a new home that does not have a history," he said.
The National Party was formed as a white nationalist group and started implementing apartheid after winning power in 1948.
In 1990 de Klerk, then state president, began dismantling apartheid. Meyer and the ANC's Cyril Ramaphosa effectively led the negotiations leading to the first all-race elections in April 1994.

The National Party came a distant second to President Nelson Mandela's ANC in the polls, having failed to broaden its support beyond the white and coloured (mixed-race) communities and is now the largest opposition party.
